requirements.requirement: Run a three-member etcd cluster across node1/node2/node3 holding application keys
requirements.summary: All three etcd v3.5.17 members reached 'started' state and passed endpoint health checks; three application keys (/app/config/db_host, /app/config/feature_flags, /app/secrets/api_key) were written and read back across the cluster.

requirements.requirement: node3 member is permanently lost (data cannot be recovered) — disruption must be demonstrated while cluster availability is preserved
requirements.summary: etcd was stopped/disabled and /var/lib/etcd wiped on node3; immediately after, node1 and node2 both reported endpoint health true and served all /app keys via quorum, directly showing bounded disruption with preserved availability.

requirements.requirement: Replace the lost node3 member with a working member on the same system so the cluster returns to three healthy members
requirements.summary: The dead member (d25d91028a25a18) was removed via etcdctl, a new member for node3 was added with the same peer URL, etcd was reconfigured/started on node3 with ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE=existing, and the resulting member list showed all 3 members in 'started' state with matching raft index (22) across endpoints — a directly observed successful transition.

requirements.requirement: Existing application keys remain intact after replacement
requirements.summary: After the new node3 member synced, a local read against 127.0.0.1:2379 on node3 returned all three original /app keys with unchanged values, confirming data was replicated intact rather than reseeded.

requirements.requirement: (Independent of task contract) run the provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on every managed node: pre-restart boot identity/health, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: For node1, node2, and node3 (the replaced member), the trace shows pre-restart boot_id and health, a reboot command with stream-closed acknowledgement, a new distinct boot_id after reboot, and post-restart confirmation of active etcd, healthy endpoints, correct 3-member list, and intact /app keys. The fixed after_executor boot-identity snapshots (node1:16c95c08..., node2:ecedd48f..., node3:345f84ed...) match the executor-reported values exactly, cross-validating the evidence.

overall_summary: The executor built a genuine 3-member etcd cluster, loaded application keys, and directly demonstrated the required failure/replacement lifecycle: node3's member was destroyed and disabled while node1/node2 retained quorum and continued serving reads, then the dead member was removed and a new member added and synced on node3, restoring a 3/3 healthy cluster with the original keys intact and verifiable locally on the rebuilt node. All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct, non-conflicting evidence. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also completed coherently for all three nodes, with boot-identity changes cross-validated against the fixed after_executor snapshot. The only notable imperfection is minor unremoved temp-file residue (release tarball/extracted binaries, reboot log) left on all three nodes, which is low severity and does not affect functionality.
limitations: Evidence for cluster health during disruption relies on etcdctl output text rather than an independent full-system snapshot at that exact moment, though it is directly observed command output rather than an executor claim.

No comparison was possible with a 'baseline' preparation phase since prepare was not enabled (after_prepare is an alias of before_prepare), so all managed-node state changes are attributable to the executor by default.
Long-running etcd bring-up logs were truncated in places (e.g., cmd-29df524441524e34), but the final state each time was independently confirmed by subsequent health/member-list checks.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all 59 chronological executor commands. All mutating actions (package/binary install, user/dir creation, systemd unit + conf writes, firewalld port openings, cluster bootstrap, member remove/add, restarts) have a clear causal role in either building the cluster, executing the required member replacement, or completing the mandated restart-evidence protocol. The initial 'systemctl enable --now etcd' timeouts on all three nodes (cmd-6b8871fc2ee34fe2, cmd-02a70c5838914197, cmd-02adcf17ffa94729) were not unnecessary mutations — they reflect a genuine bring-up ordering issue (peer ports not yet opened in firewalld) that self-resolved once firewall rules were applied, and are not troubleshooting dead-ends since the units eventually became active without further reconfiguration. Minor residue: downloaded/extracted etcd release artifacts (/tmp/etcd.tar.gz, /tmp/etcd-v3.5.17-linux-amd64/*) and /tmp/reboot.log were left on all three nodes in the final after_executor snapshot and were never cleaned up; this is low-risk, bounded, non-destructive residue but is nonetheless unremoved abandoned state. No failed services, no unsafe port exposure beyond the required etcd ports, and no damaged package state (dnf itself was untouched; etcd was installed from a binary tarball).
